story.title: Judge Rules Maurene Comey Was Unlawfully Fired from DOJ
story.summary: A federal judge has ruled that Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was unlawfully terminated from her position as a federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York. The judge ordered her reinstatement, stating that her firing by the Trump administration was illegal. Comey had worked on high-profile cases and received positive performance reviews during her tenure.

explore_lenses.label: Why does this ruling matter beyond Comey?
explore_lenses.title: Civil-service limits upheld
explore_lenses.summary: The ruling rejects the Justice Department's position that assistant U.S. attorneys may be removed at will under Article II or 28 U.S.C. § 542(b). It treats statutory civil-service and due-process protections as binding limits on the attorney general's removal authority.

claims.text: Judge Jesse Furman held that the Civil Service Reform Act's limits on removal applied to Comey and that the government conceded those limits were violated in her case.
The court concluded that Congress gave the attorney general removal authority in 28 U.S.C. § 542(b), but later imposed lawful constraints through the Civil Service Reform Act.
The Justice Department argued that prosecutors exercise delegated executive power and that Section 542(b) authorizes the attorney general to remove them without a for-cause restriction.

The Justice Department argued that prosecutors exercise delegated executive power and that Section 542(b) authorizes the attorney general to remove them without a for-cause restriction.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: This is a district-court ruling, not a final nationwide appellate precedent; its broader reach may depend on appeal outcomes and future cases.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case get to this point?
explore_lenses.title: A firing without stated cause
explore_lenses.summary: Comey was dismissed by email in July 2025 and sued two months later. The litigation moved forward in federal court after the judge rejected the government's argument that she had to use an administrative review process first.

claims.text: Comey received a July 16, 2025 termination memorandum invoking Article II and federal law; the court record says the administration later identified then-Attorney General Pam Bondi as directing the removal, with Todd Blanche later purporting to ratify it.

Comey's complaint alleged that she was fired substantially because she is James Comey's daughter or because of perceived political affiliation; the October 26 ruling did not resolve that First Amendment allegation.

The government sought dismissal on the view that the Merit Systems Protection Board, rather than a district court, should handle the dispute; Furman ruled that the government's reliance on constitutional removal power placed the case outside that required administrative route.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the reinstatement order?
explore_lenses.title: Back pay, appeal, and a remaining claim
explore_lenses.summary: The order provides retrospective employment relief rather than returning Comey to active prosecutorial work: she had already taken another job in December 2025. The Justice Department says it will appeal, while the court has requested further briefing on a remaining First Amendment count.

claims.text: Furman granted relief including retroactive reinstatement through December 20, 2025, back pay with interest and earnings, corrected service tenure, and personnel records showing that Comey resigned rather than was terminated.
Comey no longer seeks actual reinstatement because she took another job; the remedy is designed to make her whole for the period between her firing and that departure.
A Justice Department spokesperson said the department disagrees with the decision and will appeal.
The judge ordered Comey to explain by November 9, 2026, why her unresolved First Amendment claim should not be dismissed as unnecessary or speculative after the relief granted on other claims.

story_report.summary: A federal judge ruled that the Justice Department unlawfully fired former Southern District of New York prosecutor Maurene Comey in July 2025, finding that civil-service limits on her removal were violated. Judge Jesse Furman awarded retroactive relief, including back pay and corrected personnel records, rather than ordering her return to the job because she has since taken another position. The Justice Department said it disagrees with the decision and will appeal.

sections.heading: Civil-Service Limits Governed Comey Removal
sections.body: Furman concluded that Congress had authorized the attorney general to remove assistant U.S. attorneys under 28 U.S.C. § 542(b), but later constrained that authority through the Civil Service Reform Act. The court held that those statutory removal protections applied to Comey, and the government conceded that the applicable limits had not been followed in her case. The ruling rejected the administration's position that its constitutional removal authority displaced the statutory protections.

sections.heading: Comey Alleged Political Retaliation
sections.body: Comey's complaint alleged that her dismissal was substantially motivated by her status as former FBI Director James Comey's daughter or by perceived political affiliation. The termination memorandum dated July 16, 2025, invoked Article II and federal law; court records said the administration later identified then-Attorney General Pam Bondi as directing the removal, which Todd Blanche later purported to ratify. Furman did not decide whether political retaliation motivated the firing.

sections.heading: Comey Receives Retroactive Employment Relief
sections.body: The relief includes retroactive reinstatement through Dec. 20, 2025, back pay with interest and earnings, corrected service tenure, and personnel records reflecting that Comey resigned rather than was terminated. Comey no longer seeks actual reinstatement because she took another job, so the award is intended to compensate her for the interval between her firing and departure. Furman also directed her to explain by Nov. 9, 2026, why her remaining First Amendment claim should not be dismissed as unnecessary or speculative.

unresolved.text: The Justice Department has said it will appeal, leaving the ultimate status of the ruling uncertain; the final back-pay calculation and disposition of Comey's First Amendment claim also remain unresolved.

related_stories.title: Microsoft Proposes Buyouts to 60,000 Employees Amid Cost-Cutting Efforts
related_stories.summary: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to approximately 60,000 employees, which represents about a quarter of its workforce. This initiative is part of the company's strategy to reduce costs while increasing investments in artificial intelligence. The buyout offers will be available to staff globally, including those in the UK.

related_stories.title: Sudan Faces Widespread Power Outages Following RSF Drone Attacks
related_stories.summary: Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) conducted a coordinated drone strike on five power stations, leading to significant power outages across the eastern regions of the country. The attacks targeted two power stations each in Al-Jazira and Gedaref states, and one in White Nile state, affecting large areas of these regions, according to a government official.
